stated: Introduce a 4% tax on the share buyback schemes of FTSE-100 listed companies, to incentivise productive investment, job creation and economic growth.

source.quote: Introducing a 4% tax on the share buyback schemes of FTSE-100 listed companies, to incentivise productive investment, job creation and economic growth.

bearing_set.reason: The policy directly targets corporate capital allocation to incentivise productive investment and job creation over financial engineering — a real verdict on employment quality and pay is warranted.

FTSE-100 buybacks are a significant return mechanism for UK pension funds (defined-benefit and defined-contribution); taxing them at 4% plausibly affects shareholder returns and thereby pensioner wealth, earning a non-negligible verdict on security in later life.

The explicit mechanism is redirecting capital from share buybacks toward productive investment and business expansion, directly bearing on productivity, business investment, and aggregate living standards — the core O13 indicators.

A 4% levy on FTSE-100 buybacks raises material revenue (UK buybacks have run to tens of billions per year), improving the funded-vs-borrowed balance and bearing on the debt-path sustainability indicator of O12.

Buyback returns flow disproportionately to wealthier shareholders; taxing buybacks reduces capital-market income concentrated at the top and transfers it to public purposes, moving the income/wealth gap indicator that defines O14.

membership_note: Three genuine bearings: the investment-redirection hypothesis (O13), the revenue effect (O12), and the distributional incidence on capital-owners (O14). O4 was considered but the job-creation pathway is fully subsumed within the O13 productive-investment mechanism rather than a distinct labour-quality/wages effect. O11 was considered but the levy falls on companies, not household income directly; the distributional angle routes properly to O14.
